### R1 - Oracle validation (Monte Carlo vs exact)

| row | regime | n_csps | mc_runs | exact | exact_unavail | mc | se | abs_diff | diff_over_se |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| (4,2) | high | 4 | 10000 | 1 | 2.947e-09 | 1 | 0 | 2.947e-09 | n/a |
| (4,2) | high | 4 | 160000 | 1 | 2.947e-09 | 1 | 0 | 2.947e-09 | n/a |
| (9,3) | medium | 6 | 10000 | 1 | 2.345e-07 | 1 | 0 | 2.345e-07 | n/a |
| (9,3) | medium | 6 | 160000 | 1 | 2.345e-07 | 1 | 0 | 2.345e-07 | n/a |
| (14,4) | low | 8 | 10000 | 0.999509 | 4.913e-04 | 0.9999 | 9.999e-05 | 3.913e-04 | 3.91315 |
| (14,4) | low | 8 | 160000 | 0.999509 | 4.913e-04 | 0.999594 | 5.038e-05 | 8.505e-05 | 1.68812 |
| sweep max (k 1-16, m 0-8) | low | 8 | 10000 | n/a | n/a | n/a | 0.0049939 | 0.0077423 | 3.91315 |
| sweep max (k 1-16, m 0-8) | medium | 6 | 10000 | n/a | n/a | n/a | 0.00263875 | 0.00371179 | 2.26972 |
| sweep max (k 1-16, m 0-8) | high | 4 | 10000 | n/a | n/a | n/a | 9.950e-04 | 0.00104533 | 2.23111 |
| sweep max (k 1-16, m 0-8) | low | 8 | 160000 | n/a | n/a | n/a | 0.00124862 | 0.0025548 | 3.15083 |
| sweep max (k 1-16, m 0-8) | medium | 6 | 160000 | n/a | n/a | n/a | 6.628e-04 | 6.555e-04 | 2.56115 |
| sweep max (k 1-16, m 0-8) | high | 4 | 160000 | n/a | n/a | n/a | 2.574e-04 | 7.254e-04 | 2.81794 |

R1 checks the Monte Carlo (MC) availability oracle against the exact answer. Exact values use a Poisson-binomial recursion; it matches subset enumeration on small cases. Chunks go round-robin over the regime's CSPs, as in the oracle. So (9,3) and (14,4) put several chunks on one CSP, which a real deployment forbids. The availability math is still well defined, and that is all R1 tests. For (4,2) in high, exact unavailability is 2.95e-09; MC saw no failure, so the error is 2.95e-09. For (9,3) in medium, exact unavailability is 2.35e-07; MC saw no failure, so the error is 2.35e-07. For (14,4) in low, exact availability is 0.999509. MC gives 0.999900 with 10000 runs and 0.999594 with 160000 runs. The sweep covers 432 (k,m) cells over all regimes. With 160000 runs, max |MC - exact| is 2.55e-03 and max SE is 1.25e-03. Both are under the 0.005 limit. With the deployed 10000 runs, max |MC - exact| is 7.74e-03 and max SE is 4.99e-03. The worst |MC - exact|/SE is 3.91 and 3.15, so errors look like sampling noise. When MC sees no failure, SE is 0 and the ratio shows n/a.

### R2 - Exact Pareto front and knee

| regime | n | n_nondominated | k_knee | m_knee | chunk_kb_knee | A_knee | nines | overhead | repair_bw_bytes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| low | 8 | 18 | 2 | 2 | 256 | 0.9997 | 3.5 nines | 1 | 524288 |
| medium | 6 | 6 | 2 | 1 | 256 | 0.9999 | 4 nines | 0.5 | 524288 |
| high | 4 | 4 | 2 | 1 | 256 | 1 | >=4.0 nines (MC limit) | 0.5 | 524288 |

R2 is the exact Pareto front found by full enumeration, with its knee point. In low (8 CSPs) the front has 18 points. The knee is RS(2,2) with 256 KB chunks. It reaches availability 0.9997 (3.5 nines) at overhead m/k = 1.00. In medium (6 CSPs) the front has 6 points. The knee is RS(2,1) with 256 KB chunks. It reaches availability 0.9999 (4 nines) at overhead m/k = 0.50. In high (4 CSPs) the front has 4 points. The knee is RS(2,1) with 256 KB chunks. It reaches availability 1.0000 (>=4.0 nines (MC limit)) at overhead m/k = 0.50. These knees are the reference answers NSGA-II must find.

It reaches 95% of its final hypervolume after 1.9 generations. In medium, normalised hypervolume is 1.000 and IGD is 0. The knee matches the exact knee in 100% of repeats. It reaches 95% of its final hypervolume after 1.0 generations. Hypervolume near 1 and IGD near 0 mean NSGA-II recovers the exact front.

R4 simulates a fleet of 1000 stripes per regime and compares three strategies. In low, the NSGA-II knee deploys (3,3,256KB) x6, (2,2,256KB) x4. Its storage overhead is 2.00 (+33.3% vs fixed), with exact availability 0.9998208 (3.7 nines). Fixed reaches 0.9976782 (2.6 nines). Greedy deploys (5,3,256KB) x6, (4,2,256KB) x4 at overhead 1.56, exact availability 0.999217. In medium, the NSGA-II knee deploys (2,1,256KB) x10. Its storage overhead is 1.50 (+0.0% vs fixed), with exact availability 0.9999323 (4.2 nines). Fixed reaches 0.9999981 (5.7 nines). Greedy deploys (5,1,256KB) x10 at overhead 1.20, exact availability 0.9996912. In high, the NSGA-II knee deploys (2,1,256KB) x10. Its storage overhead is 1.50 (+0.0% vs fixed), with exact availability 0.9999993 (6.1 nines). Fixed RS(4,2) needs 6 CSPs, so it is infeasible in high. Greedy deploys (1,0,256KB) x10 at overhead 1.00, exact availability 0.9993621. Simulated availability saturates at >=3.0 nines (sim limit), so the exact column is the fairer comparison.

### R5 - Adaptation under drift (medium regime)

| metric | adaptive | static |
| --- | --- | --- |
| detection_latency_epochs | 1.3000 ± 0.3456 | n/a |

| pre_drift_triggers | 0.0000 ± 0.0000 | n/a |
| post_drift_triggers | 3.7000 ± 0.8954 | n/a |

R5 tests the adaptation loop in the medium regime (6 CSPs). At epoch 10, two CSPs start failing 5 times as often. After drift, adaptive availability is 0.9998 versus 0.9996 for static. Adaptive pays overhead 1.73 versus 1.50 for static. The drift is detected after 1.3 epochs on average. Before drift there are 0.0 false triggers per run on average. Re-optimising takes 29.9 s per run in total. So the controller trades some extra storage for higher availability after drift.
